Die Cast · Shot-reading chain · Verified on MPP_MES_Dev

Press Counter Review Book

Three shifts driven end to end through the real terminal, to show how the press counter credits each basket when cavities roll at different times — and when they never roll at all.

Captured 10 Sep 2026, Second Shift Terminal Die Cast 1 Operator DEV Screens Lot Release · Record Shift Output

The rule every screen below is applying

The press counter resets each shift. The operator types the reading, never an increment. Each cavity remembers the reading it was last settled at — its credited-through watermark — and a basket is credited the difference:

credit = reading − credited-through   (cavity starts each shift at 0)

A release does double duty: it closes the outgoing basket and becomes the watermark the next basket on that cavity starts from. A cavity that never rolls has one segment, 0 → R, so it is credited the whole reading — which is exactly the old uniform behaviour. Uniform fan-out is not replaced; it becomes the case where nothing rolled.

Scenario A · die RB-A · Machine 04

One cavity, ten baskets, and a partial at the buzzer

A single-cavity die filling 70-piece baskets. The basket rolls ten times in one shift, and the eleventh is still on the press when the shift ends.

READING 70

First basket of the shift

Nothing has been recorded yet, so the cavity is credited from zero and the whole reading lands on this basket.

READING 350

Fifth basket — the chain holding

Four baskets have already been settled. The counter now reads 350, but this basket is only credited what has happened since its cavity was last settled at 280.

READING 735

End of shift, with a part-full basket

The tenth basket closed at 700. The eleventh has been on the press for 35 shots. Recording shift output at 735 credits it those 35 and no more — it stays open into the next shift.

What this proves

Ten rolls on one cavity produced 735 pieces from 735 shots — one piece per shot, with no basket double-credited and nothing lost in the gaps between them. Tools.Tool.ShotCount advanced to 735 exactly once, not once per basket.

Scenario B · die RB-B · Machine 05

Four cavities, two of them rolling mid-shift

The case the old model could not express at all: two cavities swap baskets partway through the shift and two do not, so by the end of shift the four baskets on the press hold genuinely different quantities.

READING —

Shift starts with four baskets

One open basket per cavity, all on zero, all credited from zero.

READING 1450

Cavities 1 and 3 swap baskets

The operator writes down the counter at the swap and types it here. Both rolling cavities are settled at 1,450; cavities 2 and 4 are untouched and keep their watermark at zero.

NEW BASKETS

Successors opened on the two cavities that closed

New baskets go on cavities 1 and 3 only. Each inherits its cavity's watermark of 1,450 — not zero — so it cannot be credited shots that belong to the basket before it.

READING 2000

One end-of-shift entry, four different answers

This is the whole point of the model. A single reading of 2,000 produces a different credit per cavity, because each cavity is measured from where it was last settled.

Exhaust 1 Ba91000113open1,450 → 2,000550
Exhaust 2 Bb91000104open0 → 2,0002,000
Die RB-B4 cavities—2,000 shots8,000 pc

What this proves

Four cavities × 2,000 shots = 8,000 pieces, and that is exactly what the six baskets hold once the two rolled cavities are added back together (1,450 + 550 on each). The die's shot count advanced to 2,000 — once for the shift, not 1,450 + 2,000 — because the release and the shift-end entry each moved the watermark rather than adding to a running total.

Four baskets, untouched all shift

READING 1800

Uniform fan-out, arrived at rather than assumed

Every cavity is credited the full 1,800. That is the same number the old die-wide model would have produced — but here it is a result, not a rule, because each cavity genuinely has one segment from 0 to 1,800.

What this proves

The common shift is unchanged. 1,800 × 4 = 7,200 pieces from 1,800 shots, identical to what the plant would have recorded before the shot-reading chain existed — so the new model costs nothing on the shifts that make up most of the week.

Raised by this walkthrough

Three things worth a decision

Defect · Lot Release

A release dialog left open over a basket someone else closes goes to pieces

If the basket the dialog is bound to stops being Open while the dialog is up — a second terminal on the same press releases it, which is the exact case the die cast screens already refresh for — every bound field in the dialog degrades to a Component Error. The math strip reads “pc” with no number, the cavity line reads “credited through counter .”, and the operator is left looking at a dialog whose Release basket button is still enabled.

Suggested: when the preview comes back not-found, close the dialog with a toast naming the basket, rather than rendering an empty one.

Fixed · Record Shift Output

A settled basket wore its successor's credit note

On a cavity that rolled, both baskets appear in the end-of-shift list — correctly, because the closed one can still take scrap. But the closed basket (91000101, frozen at its 1,450) carries the caption “credited thru 1450 · +550 shots”, which belongs to the successor and reads as though it is about to be credited another 550.

The numbers written were always correct — the settled basket keeps its 1,450 and DieCastShiftOutput_Record rejects pieces on a closed basket outright. Only the caption described the wrong basket.

Fixed and re-verified — one label was serving three kinds of row, so it now says what is true of each. The scenario B screenshot above shows the corrected screen. released basket  —  credited thru 1450 · +550 shots released basket  —  released earlier this shift · scrap only no basket  —  no basket · 2,000 shots ran
Defect · Unrelated work in flight

Every cavity currently reads “Cavity ?”

Visible in the scenario B screenshot above, under each cavity name. A rename of CavityNumber to CavityCode has landed in the Perspective scripts but not yet in the SQL: Workorder.DieCast_GetShiftOutputBreakdown still returns a column called CavityNumber, so every r.get("CavityCode") comes back empty and the ordinal falls back to its ? placeholder.

The cavity name still reads correctly, because it comes from the description rather than the code — which is why this shows up as a cosmetic blank rather than an outright failure. The same lookup is used by the Release dialog and the bulk-open grid, so it is worth checking all three once the SQL side lands.

Nothing to do with the counter model — every figure in this book was read back from the database and is unaffected. Noted here only so the placeholder in the screenshot is not a mystery.

Carried over · Die life

A wrong reading still inflates ShotCount permanently

The counter anchor added this week lets an operator correct a wrong or reset counter, but it is forward-only by design: it sets where crediting resumes and does not claw back what a bad reading already added to Tools.Tool.ShotCount. A typo of 2124 adds 2,124 shots of phantom die life against ShotLimit.

Not exercised in these three scenarios — flagged here because die life drives maintenance, and nothing on the floor would reveal the drift.

How this was produced

Every screenshot is the live Perspective terminal at 1600×1000 against MPP_MES_Dev, driven through a real browser — sign-in, cell selection, typed counter readings, and button presses — not mocked up.

Three review dies (RB-A, RB-B, RB-C) were mounted on three idle die cast machines (DC1-M04/05/06) so that nothing already in Dev was touched. Baskets were opened with Lots.DieCastLot_Open and released with Lots.DieCastLot_Release — the same procedures the Open Basket tab and the Release dialog call. In scenario A the repetitive middle of the run (baskets 2–4 and 6–10) was fast-forwarded through those same procedures; every step shown in a screenshot was performed through the user interface.

Figures in the tables are read back from the database after the fact, not transcribed from the screens.
